title: Residual Value vs. Market Value: What the Gap Means for You
description: Your contract residual was a forecast made years ago. The market has its own opinion today. Here is how the difference decides whether buying makes sense.
body:
Two numbers decide most lease-end choices. One is printed in your contract. The other changes every week.

The residual: a forecast on paper

When you signed, the leasing company projected what your car would be worth when the lease ended and wrote that number into the contract. That projection is the residual value. It also helped set your monthly payment, since a higher residual means you pay for less depreciation.

The residual is fixed. It does not move if used-car prices jump or slump. That is exactly why it creates opportunities and problems at the end.

Market value: what someone would actually pay

Market value is what a similar car, with similar mileage and condition, would sell for right now. It depends on the model, trim, color, options, location, season, and the general state of the used market. Unlike the residual, it can change a lot over the course of a three-year lease.

The gap has a name: equity

If market value is higher than your buyout price, you have positive equity. If it is lower, you have negative equity. Everything else in this post flows from that comparison.

  • Positive equity: buying lets you keep a car that is worth more than you pay, or sell it and keep the difference.
  • Roughly even: the decision comes down to whether you like the car and what it would cost to replace it.
  • Negative equity: buying means paying more than the car is worth. Returning it may be cheaper, unless mileage or wear charges change the math.

A hypothetical to make it concrete

These numbers are invented for illustration. Suppose the buyout price is $19,500 after fees. Comparable cars in your area are listed between $21,000 and $22,500, and you would expect a dealer to offer less than retail if you sold the car. Your equity is real but smaller than the retail listings suggest, because retail and trade-in are different markets. Always compare your buyout to the number you could realistically get, not the highest ad you can find.

How to estimate market value without guessing

  1. Pull at least three sources: a pricing guide, active local listings for the same trim, and a recent offer from an instant-offer service or dealer.
  2. Adjust for mileage. Listings with 20,000 fewer miles are not comparable.
  3. Adjust for condition. Be honest about dents, curb rash, and interior wear.
  4. Throw out the highest and lowest values and look at the middle.

Why the gap can flip during the lease

Used prices respond to new-car supply, interest rates, and shifting demand for specific body styles. A contract signed in a tight market can end in a loose one, and the reverse. This is why neighbors with the same model can reach opposite conclusions.

Where this fits in the decision

Equity is only one input. Include taxes, fees, the cost of a replacement car, and whether you actually want to keep driving this one. For the fee side, read the disposition fee post. For a check on whether your finances support a purchase, see what to tidy up before you apply.

Illustrative figures only. Actual values depend on your vehicle, location, and the current market.
